title: Indian-American-Led ST LNG Wins US Approval for $8.2 Billion Texas Deepwater Port
excerpt: The Maritime Administration has licensed ST LNG's offshore liquefaction port 10.4 miles off Matagorda, Texas — four trains, 8.4 million tonnes a year, construction from 2027.
body:
• The US Maritime Administration (MARAD) has approved a deepwater port licence for ST LNG, LLC, the Indian-American-led developer planning an $8.2 billion liquefied natural gas port off Matagorda, Texas.
  • The port will have four liquefaction systems of 2.1 million tonnes per annum each — 8.4 mtpa in total — and is expected to expand US LNG export capacity by 7-9%.
  • The Transportation Department says the project will support 2,000 construction jobs and up to 855 permanent jobs.
  • Construction is expected to begin in 2027, with the port coming online in 2029.

The United States has approved a deepwater port licence for ST LNG, LLC, clearing the central regulatory hurdle for an $8.2 billion offshore liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminal to be built about 10.4 miles offshore Matagorda, Texas. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy announced the Maritime Administration's approval, and The Economic Times reported the developer is Indian-American-led, with chief executive Sharad Tak among those welcoming the decision.

"By slashing red tape and modernizing our licensing processes, the Trump Administration is delivering a massive economic boom for the people of Texas. This project will unleash American energy."

— Sean P. Duffy, US Transportation Secretary

What will be built

At full capacity, the port will include four liquefaction systems of 2.1 million tonnes per annum each, for a combined 8.4 million tonnes a year, along with 20 platforms, four LNG floating storage units, four mooring systems and 7.7 miles of pipeline, according to the Transportation Department's announcement, carried in full by Marine Insight. Feed gas will come from the Tres Palacios Natural Gas Storage and Trading Hub and the Williams Markham Gas Processing Plant through an existing Transco pipeline about 5.6 miles northeast of the port. Siting the terminal offshore is expected to move vessel traffic away from more congested onshore areas, reducing collision and safety risks.

Jobs and capacity

The department projects 2,000 construction jobs and up to 855 permanent positions, and says the port would expand America's LNG export capacity by 7-9%. MARAD Administrator Stephen M. Carmel said it was the agency's third deepwater port approval under the Trump administration. The full Record of Decision and related documents are filed under Docket Number MARAD-2025-0096, according to DredgeWire's report of the announcement.

The licence also closes an unusually fast federal review: reporting on the approval noted the project's final environmental impact review was completed in 410 days. MARAD handled the application jointly with the US Coast Guard, other federal agencies and the State of Texas, and the construction and operating decision now sits in federal docket MARAD-2025-0096.

What happens next

Construction is expected to begin in 2027, with the port coming online in 2029. Those dates are the developer's and the department's stated schedule, not a completion guarantee: offshore installation, final engineering and procurement still lie ahead. For the Texas Gulf Coast's large Indian-American energy workforce, the project is one of the biggest single additions to US export infrastructure this decade — and a rare case of an Indian-American-led firm carrying a project of this scale through federal licensing.
